1-1.text: Part one. What is pressure? ... Pressure is about how spread out a force is. These two bricks weigh the same. One stands on its end and one lies flat on a soft sponge.

1-2.text: On its end, the brick pushes on a small area, so the pressure is big and it sinks in deep. Lying flat, the same weight is spread over a big area, so the pressure is small.

1-3.text: A drawing pin has a tiny point. The small area makes a huge pressure, so it goes into the board easily. The wide flat head spreads the force on your thumb.

1-4.text: Snowshoes do the opposite. They spread your weight over a big area, so the pressure on the snow is small and you don't sink in.

2-1.text: Part two. Calculating pressure. ... To work out pressure: pressure equals force divided by area. The force is in newtons. The area is in square metres.

2-2.text: So pressure is measured in newtons per square metre. Another name for 1 newton per square metre is 1 pascal.

2-3.text: A crate weighing 200 newtons lies on 4 square metres of floor. Pressure equals 200 divided by 4, which is 50 newtons per square metre. Each square metre of floor gets 50 newtons.

2-4.text: Turn the crate onto a smaller side, with an area of 2 square metres. Now the same 200 newtons is shared by only 2 squares. Pressure equals 200 divided by 2, which is 100 newtons per square metre. Half the area, double the pressure!

3-1.text: Part three. Pressure in liquids and gases. ... Liquids and gases press on every surface they touch, in all directions: down, up and sideways.

3-2.text: The deeper you go, the more water there is above you, pushing down. So water pressure increases with depth. Water squirts out hardest from the lowest hole.

3-3.text: That's why a dam is built much thicker at the bottom. The water pushes hardest at the bottom, so that part must be strongest.

3-4.text: Air has pressure too, because of all the air above pressing down. High up a mountain there is less air above you, so the air pressure is lower.

4-1.text: Part four. Moments: forces that turn. ... Forces can make things turn. The point something turns around is called the pivot. Here the pivot is the nut in the middle.

4-2.text: The turning effect of a force is called a moment. To work it out: moment equals force times distance from the pivot.

4-3.text: A 20 newton force pushes 3 metres from the pivot. Its moment is 20 times 3, which is 60 newton metres.

4-4.text: A bigger distance gives a bigger moment. That's why you push a door near the handle, far from the hinge. Pushing near the hinge is much harder.

5-1.text: Part five. Balancing a see-saw. ... On a see-saw, each weight tries to turn it. The 30 newton block on the left tries to turn it anticlockwise. The 20 newton block on the right tries to turn it clockwise.

5-2.text: Left: 30 newtons times 2 metres is 60 newton metres. Right: 20 newtons times 3 metres is also 60 newton metres.

5-3.text: The moments are equal, so the see-saw balances. This is the principle of moments: it balances when the clockwise and anticlockwise moments are equal.

5-4.text: So a lighter person can balance a heavier person by sitting further from the pivot.
